pharm-gi:gimap.q: Which receptor do ondansetron and granisetron block?
pharm-gi:gimap.e: Central and peripheral 5-HT₃ antagonism prevents emesis.

o: Binding the ulcer base as a protective barrier
Blocking H₂ receptors on parietal cells
pharm-gi:gimap.e: Needs acid to polymerize; avoid with PPIs.

pharm-gi:gimap.q: A 55-year-old man receiving cisplatin is given an IV antiemetic before each cycle. He later reports headache and constipation, and his QTc is 500 ms. Which receptor does this drug block?
pharm-gi:gimap.e: Ondansetron (5-HT₃ antagonist) causes headache, constipation and QT prolongation. NK₁ antagonists (aprepitant) are added for delayed emesis.

pharm-gi:acid.e: Gynecomastia, impotence; crosses BBB and placenta.
Proton pumps are activated by meals.

pharm-gi:acid.q: A 61-year-old man on stable warfarin buys an over-the-counter drug for heartburn. Four weeks later his INR has risen from 2.4 to 4.6 and he has tender breast enlargement. Which drug did he most likely start?
pharm-gi:acid.e: Cimetidine inhibits CYP450 (↑ warfarin) and has antiandrogen effects causing gynecomastia. Famotidine has neither effect to a meaningful degree.

pharm-gi:mucosal.e: Aluminum hydroxide constipates; calcium carbonate can cause hypercalcemia.
Uterine contraction; also used for medical abortion and labor induction.

pharm-gi:mucosal.q: A 64-year-old man with a benign gastric ulcer is prescribed a drug that forms a viscous gel adhering to the ulcer base. Which concurrently prescribed drug would most reduce its effectiveness?
pharm-gi:mucosal.e: Sucralfate needs an acidic pH to polymerize, so acid suppression with a PPI reduces its effect. Amoxicillin does not alter gastric pH.

pharm-gi:octreotide.e: Used for variceal bleeding, acromegaly, carcinoid and VIPoma.

pharm-gi:octreotide.q: A long-term adverse effect of octreotide:

A 58-year-old man has episodic facial flushing, watery diarrhea and wheezing. Echocardiography shows tricuspid regurgitation, urinary 5-HIAA is elevated and CT shows multiple liver metastases. Which drug is best for controlling his symptoms?
pharm-gi:octreotide.e: Carcinoid syndrome is controlled with a somatostatin analog, which inhibits release of serotonin and other tumor hormones. Loperamide treats diarrhea only, not flushing.

pharm-gi:ibd.q: Sulfasalazine is cleaved by colonic bacteria into:
pharm-gi:ibd.e: Sulfapyridine causes oligospermia and sulfa toxicity.

pharm-gi:ibd.q: For moderate–severe Crohn disease, which biologic is used?
pharm-gi:ibd.e: Anti-TNF; screen for latent TB first.

pharm-gi:ibd.q: A 29-year-old man with fistulizing Crohn disease is about to start infliximab. He was born in a country with high tuberculosis prevalence. Which test should be done before the first dose?
pharm-gi:ibd.e: TNF-α blockade can reactivate latent TB, so screen with IGRA or tuberculin skin test. TPMT activity is checked before azathioprine/6-MP.

pharm-gi:antidiar.e: Poor CNS penetration; low addictive potential; slows intestinal motility.

pharm-gi:antidiar.q: Antimotility agents should be avoided in:
pharm-gi:antidiar.e: Risk of toxic megacolon or HUS. Examples: C. difficile, Shiga toxin–producing E. coli.

pharm-gi:antidiar.q: A 32-year-old woman with diarrhea-predominant IBS uses an over-the-counter μ-opioid agonist that slows gut transit. At usual doses she has no sedation or euphoria. Which property best explains the lack of CNS effects?
pharm-gi:antidiar.e: Loperamide is pumped out of the CNS by P-glycoprotein, so effects stay peripheral. It is a μ (not κ) agonist.

pharm-gi:antiemetic.e: Used for gastroparesis; causes EPS and tardive dyskinesia.
Added for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

pharm-gi:antiemetic.q: A 47-year-old woman with diabetic gastroparesis has taken a prokinetic drug for 5 months. She now has involuntary lip-smacking and tongue-thrusting movements. Blockade at which site explains this effect?
o: D₂ receptors in the nigrostriatal tract
M₁ receptors in the basal ganglia
H₁ receptors in the vomiting center
pharm-gi:antiemetic.e: Metoclopramide blocks D₂ receptors, causing tardive dyskinesia with long use (limit to ≤ 12 weeks). 5-HT₄ agonism is a prokinetic mechanism, not a cause of dyskinesia.

pharm-gi:laxative.q: Lactulose is used in hepatic encephalopathy because it:
o: Is converted by gut flora to acids that trap NH₄⁺
Acts as a stimulant laxative like senna
pharm-gi:laxative.e: Osmotic laxative; rifaximin is often added.
Peripheral μ antagonist that does not cross the BBB.

pharm-gi:laxative.q: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis becomes confused 2 days after a variceal bleed. He has asterixis and plasma ammonia 140 µmol/L. Which mechanism underlies the first-line drug for his condition?
pharm-gi:laxative.e: Lactulose is metabolized by colonic bacteria to acids that convert NH₃ to non-absorbable NH₄⁺ and act as an osmotic laxative. It does not act on hepatic ammonia metabolism.

o: Agonizing GLP-1 receptors to slow emptying

pharm-gi:orlistat.q: A GLP-1 agonist approved for weight loss:
pharm-gi:orlistat.e: Liraglutide and semaglutide; GI side effects.

pharm-gi:orlistat.q: A 38-year-old woman with obesity began a weight-loss drug 6 months ago and reports oily stools and fecal urgency after fatty meals. She now has difficulty seeing in dim light. Which supplement should have been advised?
o: Vitamins A, D, E and K
pharm-gi:orlistat.e: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipase, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (vitamin A → night blindness). B12 absorption is unaffected.

pharm-gi:pud.e: Gastrinoma causes refractory ulcers; resect if possible.

pharm-gi:pud.q: First-line therapy for GERD with erosive esophagitis:
pharm-gi:pud.e: PPIs heal esophagitis better than H₂ blockers.

pharm-gi:pud.q: A 71-year-old woman with severe knee osteoarthritis must continue daily naproxen. She had a bleeding gastric ulcer last year; H. pylori testing is negative. Which strategy best reduces her risk of recurrent ulcer?
o: Add an antacid after each meal
Add a daily proton pump inhibitor
pharm-gi:pud.e: PPIs (or misoprostol) effectively prevent NSAID-induced ulcers. Standard-dose H₂ blockers prevent duodenal but not gastric NSAID ulcers.

pharm-gi:cirrhosis.q: Nonselective β-blocker used to prevent variceal bleeding:
Diuretic of choice for cirrhotic ascites:
A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis has medium-sized esophageal varices without prior bleeding and is started on propranolol rather than metoprolol. Which effect of β₂ blockade explains this choice?
o: Direct relaxation of hepatic stellate cells
pharm-gi:cirrhosis.e: Nonselective β-blockers lower cardiac output (β₁) and, via β₂ blockade, allow unopposed α₁ splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal inflow. They do not affect ammonia clearance.

gi-patho-1:oral.q: A white oral patch that cannot be scraped off and has no other clinical explanation is called:
gi-patho-1:oral.e: By definition, scrapable plaques (candidiasis) and recognizable diseases are excluded; all leukoplakias need biopsy.

gi-patho-1:oral.q: Which oral lesion carries the highest likelihood of dysplasia or carcinoma at biopsy?
gi-patho-1:oral.e: About 90% of erythroplakias show severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma.

gi-patho-1:oral.q: A 34-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has painless, white, vertically corrugated plaques on the lateral borders of his tongue that cannot be scraped off. The responsible agent is:
gi-patho-1:oral.e: Hairy leukoplakia is caused by EBV in immunosuppressed patients and is not premalignant.

gi-patho-1:salivary.q: The most common salivary gland neoplasm is the:
gi-patho-1:salivary.e: It makes up about 60% of parotid tumors and contains epithelial, myoepithelial and chondromyxoid elements.

gi-patho-1:salivary.q: A tumor of which gland is most likely to be malignant?
gi-patho-1:salivary.e: The smaller the gland, the higher the proportion of malignant tumors (70–90% for sublingual vs about 50% for minor glands).

gi-patho-1:salivary.q: A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years has a slow-growing, painless mass near the angle of the mandible on both sides. Biopsy shows cystic spaces lined by a double layer of oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid tissue with germinal centers. The diagnosis is:
gi-patho-1:salivary.e: Warthin tumor: almost always parotid, smokers, sometimes bilateral or multifocal.

gi-patho-1:achalasia.q: Primary achalasia results from loss of which neurons in the myenteric plexus?
o: Inhibitory neurons that release nitric oxide
Sensory neurons that release substance P
gi-patho-1:achalasia.e: Loss of NO/VIP-mediated relaxation leaves the LES unable to relax; the esophageal body becomes aperistaltic.

gi-patho-1:achalasia.q: Esophageal manometry in achalasia typically shows:
o: Low LES pressure with absent peristalsis
High LES pressure with absent peristalsis
Normal LES pressure with simultaneous contractions
gi-patho-1:achalasia.e: Low LES pressure with weak peristalsis is the scleroderma pattern; simultaneous contractions are esophageal spasm.

gi-patho-1:achalasia.q: A 30-year-old man who grew up in rural Brazil has progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food and chronic constipation. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a narrow distal segment. The underlying mechanism is:
o: Eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa
Autoimmune fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle
Parasitic destruction of enteric ganglion cells
Malignant infiltration of the gastroesophageal junction
gi-patho-1:achalasia.e: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) destroys the myenteric plexus of the esophagus and colon.

gi-patho-1:gerd.q: The main mechanism of gastroesophageal reflux is:
o: Delayed relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter
Loss of esophageal peristalsis from denervation
Hypersecretion of acid by parietal cells
Transient relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
gi-patho-1:gerd.e: Vagally mediated transient LES relaxations, triggered by gastric distention.

gi-patho-1:gerd.q: Linear, superficial esophageal ulcers with inclusions in endothelial and stromal cells at the ulcer base indicate:
gi-patho-1:gerd.e: HSV causes small punched-out ulcers with inclusions in epithelial cells at the margins; Candida forms white pseudomembranes.

gi-patho-1:gerd.q: A 19-year-old man with asthma and allergic rhinitis had a piece of steak lodge in his esophagus. He did not improve with 8 weeks of PPI therapy. Endoscopy shows stacked circular rings and linear furrows. Biopsy will most likely show:
gi-patho-1:gerd.e: Eosinophilic esophagitis; treat with allergen elimination and topical corticosteroids.

gi-patho-1:barrett.q: The cell type whose presence confirms Barrett esophagus on biopsy is the:
gi-patho-1:barrett.e: Intestinal-type metaplasia with goblet cells replaces squamous mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction.

gi-patho-1:barrett.q: Barrett esophagus is the main precursor of:
gi-patho-1:barrett.e: Most esophageal adenocarcinomas arise in Barrett mucosa, although most Barrett patients never develop cancer.

gi-patho-1:barrett.q: A 58-year-old obese man has had heartburn for 15 years. Endoscopy shows salmon-pink, velvety mucosa extending 5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsies show crowded glands with hyperchromatic, stratified nuclei extending to the surface and gland-within-gland profiles, but no invasion of the lamina propria. This finding is best classified as:
gi-patho-1:barrett.e: Cribriform architecture without lamina propria invasion is high-grade dysplasia; invasion would make it intramucosal carcinoma.

gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.q: Esophageal varices are dilated veins that drain portal blood mainly through the:
o: Paraumbilical veins to the epigastric veins
Left gastric vein to the azygos system
Splenic vein to the left renal vein
Superior rectal vein to the inferior rectal veins
gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.e: Portal hypertension reverses flow in the left gastric vein into esophageal veins.

gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.q: Which feature distinguishes Boerhaave syndrome from a Mallory-Weiss tear?
o: Transmural rupture of the esophageal wall
gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.e: Mallory-Weiss tears are limited to mucosa/submucosa; Boerhaave ruptures the full thickness, causing mediastinitis.

gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.q: After a night of binge drinking, a 24-year-old man vomited repeatedly and then brought up bright red blood. He is hemodynamically stable. Endoscopy shows a 1-cm longitudinal mucosal laceration straddling the gastroesophageal junction. The expected course is:
gi-patho-1:esoph-tears.e: Mallory-Weiss tears usually stop bleeding spontaneously and heal rapidly.

gi-patho-1:dysphagia.q: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from onset suggests:
gi-patho-1:dysphagia.e: Mechanical obstruction affects solids first; motility disorders affect both.

gi-patho-1:dysphagia.q: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is the combination of upper esophageal webs with:
gi-patho-1:dysphagia.e: It increases the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

gi-patho-1:dysphagia.q: A 72-year-old man has had 3 months of worsening difficulty swallowing meat, now also bread, and has lost 8 kg. He has smoked and drunk heavily for decades. The best initial test is:
gi-patho-1:dysphagia.e: Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss suggests carcinoma; EGD visualizes and biopsies the lesion.

gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.q: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma most often arises in the:
gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.e: About half arise in the middle third; adenocarcinoma is distal.

gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.q: Which risk factor is associated with esophageal adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma?
gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.e: Obesity-related GERD and Barrett esophagus drive adenocarcinoma; the others are squamous risk factors.

gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.q: A 66-year-old man who drinks heavily and smokes has progressive dysphagia and weight loss. He now coughs every time he drinks water, and has recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia. The most likely explanation is:
o: Tumor extension forming a tracheoesophageal fistula
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy from goiter
gi-patho-1:esoph-ca.e: Mid-esophageal squamous cell carcinoma can invade the trachea.

gi-patho-1:gastritis.q: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis typically shows which combination?
o: Increased acid with low serum gastrin
gi-patho-1:gastritis.e: Parietal cell loss removes acid feedback, so G cells in the spared antrum hypersecrete gastrin.

gi-patho-1:gastritis.q: Ulcers that arise in a patient with severe burns are called:
gi-patho-1:gastritis.e: Curling ulcers follow burns/trauma (hypovolemia, ischemia); Cushing ulcers follow intracranial injury (vagal acid hypersecretion).

gi-patho-1:gastritis.q: A 64-year-old woman with vitiligo has fatigue, a smooth red tongue and decreased vibration sense in her feet. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL with MCV 118 fL. Gastric biopsy would most likely show:
o: Diffuse foveolar hyperplasia with giant rugae
Antral gastritis with curved surface bacilli
Body and fundus atrophy with a spared antrum
Multiple shallow erosions with brown bases
gi-patho-1:gastritis.e: Autoimmune gastritis causes pernicious anemia; antibodies target parietal cells and intrinsic factor.

gi-patho-1:menetrier.q: Ménétrier disease is caused by excessive secretion of:
gi-patho-1:menetrier.e: TGF-α activates the EGF receptor, driving foveolar hyperplasia.

gi-patho-1:menetrier.q: The hypoalbuminemia of Ménétrier disease results from:
o: Protein loss across the gastric mucosa
gi-patho-1:menetrier.e: Protein-losing gastropathy can lose up to about 10 g of albumin per day.

gi-patho-1:menetrier.q: A 52-year-old man has epigastric pain, weight loss and leg edema. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL; urine has no protein and liver tests are normal. Endoscopy shows massively enlarged, brain-like rugal folds in the body and fundus with a normal antrum. Biopsy would show:
o: Foveolar hyperplasia with tortuous, cystic glands
Parietal cell hyperplasia with deep gland elongation
Signet-ring cells infiltrating the gastric wall
gi-patho-1:menetrier.e: Ménétrier disease; parietal cell hyperplasia is the Zollinger-Ellison pattern.

gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.q: Loss of E-cadherin is characteristic of which gastric cancer?
gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.e: Germline CDH1 mutations cause familial diffuse cancer; discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrate the wall.

gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.q: A metastatic deposit in a periumbilical skin nodule is called a:
gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.e: Virchow = left supraclavicular node; Krukenberg = ovaries; Blumer shelf = rectouterine pouch.

gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.q: A 47-year-old woman has early satiety and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass. Six months later bilateral ovarian masses are found. Microscopy of both lesions shows:
o: Small B cells forming lymphoepithelial lesions
Spindle cells strongly positive for KIT
gi-patho-1:gastric-ca.e: Diffuse gastric carcinoma (linitis plastica) with Krukenberg tumors.

gi-patho-1:pud.q: Which H. pylori product lets the organism survive gastric acid by generating ammonia?
gi-patho-1:pud.e: Ammonia buffers the local environment; ammonium also injures epithelium.

gi-patho-1:pud.q: Compared with gastric ulcers, duodenal ulcers are:
o: More strongly associated with H. pylori
More often on the lesser curvature
gi-patho-1:pud.e: About 90% of duodenal ulcers vs about 70% of gastric ulcers are associated with H. pylori.

gi-patho-1:pud.q: A 52-year-old man has burning epigastric pain that comes 2 hours after meals and wakes him at night; eating relieves it, and he has gained weight. He takes no medications. Which test is most appropriate next?
gi-patho-1:pud.e: A duodenal ulcer pattern without NSAID use points to H. pylori; test noninvasively (urea breath test or stool antigen).

gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.q: The most common complication of peptic ulcer disease is:
gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.e: Perforation causes most ulcer-related deaths but is less common than bleeding.

gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.q: Bleeding from a posterior duodenal ulcer usually comes from the:
gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.e: Lesser curvature gastric ulcers erode the left gastric artery.

gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.q: A 61-year-old woman taking naproxen for osteoarthritis has sudden severe epigastric pain that spreads over her abdomen and to her right shoulder. Her abdomen is rigid. An upright chest radiograph would most likely show:
o: An air–fluid level behind the heart
gi-patho-1:ulcer-cx.e: Perforated (usually anterior duodenal) ulcer: pneumoperitoneum; shoulder pain from phrenic nerve irritation.

gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.q: Upper GI bleeding is defined as bleeding proximal to the:
gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.e: The ligament of Treitz marks the duodenojejunal flexure.

gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.q: Which laboratory finding favors an upper rather than lower GI source of bleeding?
gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.e: Digested blood proteins are absorbed in the small intestine and volume depletion raises BUN.

gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.q: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large amount of bright red blood. Pulse is 118/min and BP 92/58 mm Hg. Two large-bore IV lines are placed. Besides volume resuscitation, what should be started before endoscopy?
o: Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma
gi-patho-1:gi-bleed.e: Suspected variceal bleeding: vasoactive drug plus antibiotic prophylaxis, then band ligation within 12–24 h.

gi-patho-1:gastric-polyps.q: Fundic gland polyps are most often associated with:
gi-patho-1:gastric-polyps.e: They also occur in FAP and MUTYH-associated polyposis.
GISTs express KIT (CD117) and often respond to imatinib.

gi-patho-1:gastric-polyps.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia has a 1.8-cm polyp in the gastric antrum. Biopsy shows tubular glands with elongated, hyperchromatic, stratified nuclei. The most appropriate management is:
gi-patho-1:gastric-polyps.e: Gastric adenomas frequently harbor adenocarcinoma, so they are removed.

gi-patho-2:celiac.q: The most sensitive serologic test for celiac disease is IgA antibody against:
gi-patho-2:celiac.e: Use IgG anti-tTG if the patient is IgA deficient.

gi-patho-2:celiac.q: Which HLA alleles are carried by almost all patients with celiac disease?
gi-patho-2:celiac.e: Their absence has a high negative predictive value.

gi-patho-2:celiac.q: A 34-year-old woman has fatigue, bloating and iron deficiency anemia that does not respond to oral iron. She has an intensely itchy vesicular rash on her elbows and knees. Duodenal biopsy would most likely show:
o: Foamy macrophages filling the lamina propria
Normal villi with absent brush-border lactase
gi-patho-2:celiac.e: Celiac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis; intraepithelial lymphocytosis is also present.

gi-patho-2:malabs.q: A normal D-xylose absorption test in a patient with steatorrhea points to:
gi-patho-2:malabs.e: D-xylose needs intact mucosa but no pancreatic digestion.

gi-patho-2:malabs.q: Lactase deficiency causes diarrhea that is best classified as:
gi-patho-2:malabs.e: Undigested lactose holds water in the lumen; bacterial fermentation lowers stool pH and makes gas.

gi-patho-2:malabs.q: A 58-year-old farmer has had migratory joint pains for 3 years and now has diarrhea, weight loss, and memory problems. Small-bowel biopsy shows lamina propria macrophages packed with PAS-positive, diastase-resistant granules; acid-fast stain is negative. The best treatment is:
gi-patho-2:malabs.e: Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei); mycobacterial infection would be acid-fast positive.

gi-patho-2:ibd.q: Which finding favors Crohn disease over ulcerative colitis?
gi-patho-2:ibd.e: Granulomas occur in about 35% of Crohn cases and never in ulcerative colitis.

gi-patho-2:ibd.q: The risk of colorectal carcinoma in ulcerative colitis rises most with:
o: Onset after the age of 60 years
Disease limited to the rectum only
gi-patho-2:ibd.e: Duration, extent and severity of inflammation determine risk; surveillance starts about 8 years after onset.

gi-patho-2:ibd.q: A 24-year-old man who smokes has had right lower quadrant pain, non-bloody diarrhea and weight loss for 6 months. He now passes air in his urine and has recurrent urinary infections. The most likely underlying process is:
o: Mucosal inflammation limited to the colon
Outpouching of mucosa through the muscularis
gi-patho-2:ibd.e: Crohn disease with an enterovesical fistula.

gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.q: Collagenous colitis is diagnosed by finding:
gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.e: Endoscopy is normal; biopsy also shows increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.q: Irritable bowel syndrome is characterized by:
o: Recurrent abdominal pain with normal histology
Chronic watery diarrhea with a collagen band
gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.e: It is a functional disorder diagnosed by symptom criteria after excluding organic disease.

gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.q: A 67-year-old woman has had 4 months of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, 6 times daily, including at night. She has not lost weight. She takes a daily NSAID. Colonoscopy looks normal. The next step is:
o: Stool test for fecal occult blood
gi-patho-2:ibs-mc.e: Microscopic colitis is a histologic diagnosis; nocturnal symptoms and onset after 50 argue against IBS.

gi-patho-2:appendicitis.q: The initial periumbilical pain of appendicitis is carried by:
o: Parasympathetic fibers of the vagus nerve
Visceral afferent fibers entering at T8–T10
Somatic fibers of the right phrenic nerve
Somatic fibers of the iliohypogastric nerve
gi-patho-2:appendicitis.e: Pain localizes to the right lower quadrant once the parietal peritoneum is irritated.

gi-patho-2:appendicitis.q: The histologic criterion for acute appendicitis is neutrophils within the:

A 17-year-old boy has 18 hours of abdominal pain that began around the navel and is now sharp in the right lower quadrant. Pressing on the left lower quadrant reproduces pain on the right. Temperature is 38.1 °C. The usual initiating event in an adult with this condition is:
gi-patho-2:appendicitis.e: Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and impairs venous outflow (Rovsing sign described).

gi-patho-2:diverticula.q: Colonic diverticula are classified as false diverticula because they lack:
gi-patho-2:diverticula.e: Mucosa and submucosa herniate where vasa recta pierce the circular muscle.

o: The taeniae coli of the sigmoid colon
The vitelline duct remnant of the ileum
The esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm
gi-patho-2:diverticula.e: A false diverticulum of the hypopharynx in older men.

gi-patho-2:diverticula.q: A 3-year-old boy passes a large amount of painless maroon stool. He is pale and tachycardic; the abdomen is soft. Which test is most likely to reveal the source?
gi-patho-2:diverticula.e: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa takes up pertechnetate.

gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.q: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of migration of:
gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.e: Both Meissner and Auerbach plexuses are absent in the distal segment.

gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.q: In Hirschsprung disease, the aganglionic segment always includes the:
gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.e: Aganglionosis extends proximally from the rectum for a variable distance.

gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.q: A term newborn with trisomy 21 has not passed meconium by 60 hours of life and has bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. Rectal examination produces an explosive release of stool and gas. The diagnostic test is:
gi-patho-2:hirschsprung.e: Absent ganglion cells confirm Hirschsprung disease; RET mutations are the commonest genetic cause.

gi-patho-2:obstruction.q: The most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults is:
Volvulus in adults most often involves the:
gi-patho-2:obstruction.e: A long, redundant sigmoid twists on its mesentery; the cecum is next.

gi-patho-2:obstruction.q: A previously well 10-month-old boy has episodes of screaming with his knees drawn up, vomiting, and a stool that looks like red jelly. A sausage-shaped mass is felt in the right abdomen. Ultrasound shows a target sign. Initial management is:
gi-patho-2:obstruction.e: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception; enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

gi-patho-2:ischemia.q: Which part of the colon is a watershed zone between the SMA and IMA?
gi-patho-2:ischemia.e: The rectosigmoid junction is the second watershed area.

gi-patho-2:ischemia.q: The morphologic signature of ischemic injury in the intestinal mucosa is:
o: Surface epithelial atrophy with preserved crypts
gi-patho-2:ischemia.e: Capillaries run from crypt to surface, so the surface is most vulnerable.

gi-patho-2:ischemia.q: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant has sudden, severe diffuse abdominal pain. Her abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness. Lactate is 6 mmol/L. The most likely cause is:
o: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the celiac trunk
Embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
gi-patho-2:ischemia.e: Acute mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion to examination.

gi-patho-2:angio-other.q: Angiodysplasia is found most often in the:
gi-patho-2:angio-other.e: The cecum has the widest diameter and highest wall tension.

gi-patho-2:angio-other.q: Which condition predisposes to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth?
gi-patho-2:angio-other.e: Stasis, low acid, dysmotility and IgA deficiency all favor overgrowth.

gi-patho-2:angio-other.q: A 79-year-old man with a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids has recurrent painless bleeding per rectum and iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy shows flat, cherry-red, fern-like lesions in the cecum. The lesions are:
o: Dysplastic glands on a fibrovascular stalk
gi-patho-2:angio-other.e: Angiodysplasia associated with aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome).

gi-patho-2:polyps.q: The defining histologic feature of a colonic adenoma is:
The feature of an adenoma that correlates best with the risk of cancer is its:
gi-patho-2:polyps.e: Cancer is rare in adenomas under 1 cm; villous architecture and high-grade dysplasia add risk.

gi-patho-2:polyps.q: A 62-year-old woman has a flat, 1.5-cm lesion with a mucus cap in the ascending colon. Histology shows serrated crypts that are dilated and spread sideways at their bases, without conventional dysplasia. The molecular pathway most associated with this lesion is:
o: Biallelic APC loss with KRAS mutation
CpG island methylation with BRAF mutation
gi-patho-2:polyps.e: Sessile serrated lesion: MLH1 promoter methylation leads to microsatellite instability.

gi-patho-2:polyposis.q: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by a germline mutation in:
gi-patho-2:polyposis.e: Autosomal dominant; APC is a negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.

gi-patho-2:polyposis.q: Which polyposis syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern?
gi-patho-2:polyposis.e: Biallelic loss of a base-excision repair gene; fewer than 100 polyps.

gi-patho-2:polyposis.q: A 15-year-old girl has an episode of intussusception. She has dark brown macules on her lips and buccal mucosa. Resected small bowel contains a large polyp with branching bands of smooth muscle covered by normal-appearing epithelium. She has an increased lifetime risk of:
gi-patho-2:polyposis.e: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11): hamartomatous polyps with about 40% lifetime cancer risk.

gi-patho-2:lynch.q: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in genes responsible for:
gi-patho-2:lynch.e: Most often MSH2 or MLH1, producing microsatellite instability.

gi-patho-2:lynch.q: Compared with sporadic cancers, colon cancers in Lynch syndrome are more often:
gi-patho-2:lynch.e: They occur at younger ages and tend to be mucinous with lymphocytic infiltrates.

gi-patho-2:lynch.q: A 41-year-old woman has a cecal adenocarcinoma. Her mother had endometrial cancer at 46 and her maternal uncle colon cancer at 44. Colonoscopy shows only two other small polyps. Immunostaining of the tumor would most likely show:
o: Loss of MLH1 or MSH2 expression
gi-patho-2:lynch.e: Lynch syndrome: few polyps, early cancers of colon, endometrium and ovary.

gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.q: In the classic adenoma–carcinoma sequence, the earliest genetic event is loss of:
gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.e: Both APC alleles must be inactivated for an adenoma to form.

gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.q: Loss of APC promotes proliferation by allowing nuclear accumulation of:
gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.e: β-catenin binds TCF and activates MYC and cyclin D1.

gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.q: A 2.5-cm villous adenoma is removed from the sigmoid colon. Focally, dysplastic glands invade through the muscularis mucosae into the stalk. Compared with the surrounding adenoma, the invasive focus is most likely to have acquired a mutation in:
gi-patho-2:adeno-ca.e: TP53 is mutated in 70–80% of carcinomas but rarely in adenomas, marking the late transition.

gi-patho-2:crc.q: Colorectal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes to the:
gi-patho-2:crc.e: Portal venous drainage carries tumor cells to the liver first.

gi-patho-2:crc.q: Serum CEA in colorectal cancer is most useful for:
gi-patho-2:crc.e: It is neither sensitive nor specific enough for screening.

gi-patho-2:crc.q: A 68-year-old man has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, MCV 71 fL and ferritin 6 ng/mL. He has no change in bowel habits and no visible blood in stool. The most likely finding on colonoscopy is:
o: Continuous friable mucosa from the rectum
A napkin-ring lesion in the sigmoid colon
An exophytic mass in the ascending colon
gi-patho-2:crc.e: Right-sided cancers bleed occultly and rarely obstruct; iron deficiency in an older man is GI cancer until proven otherwise.

gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.q: Esophageal varices form through collaterals between the left gastric vein and the:
gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.e: Paraumbilical–epigastric collaterals give caput medusae; superior–inferior rectal collaterals give anorectal varices.

gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.q: The increased portal inflow of cirrhosis is driven mainly by:
o: Obstruction of the main hepatic veins
Reduced oncotic pressure from low albumin
Splanchnic arterial vasodilation from nitric oxide
gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.e: Hyperdynamic circulation adds to the raised sinusoidal resistance.

gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.q: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and tense ascites has a rising creatinine and urine output of 300 mL/day. Urinalysis is bland, urine sodium is < 10 mEq/L and there is no improvement after stopping diuretics and giving albumin. Renal ultrasound is normal. The kidneys, if transplanted into another person, would most likely:
gi-patho-3:cirrhosis.e: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure from splanchnic vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction.

gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.q: Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by obstruction of the:
gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.e: Outflow obstruction produces centrilobular congestion and necrosis.

gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.q: Which lobular zone bears the brunt of injury in hepatic venous outflow obstruction?
gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.e: Congestion and necrosis are centrilobular, giving a nutmeg appearance.

gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.q: A 39-year-old woman with a hematocrit of 59% and itching after hot showers develops abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and ascites over 2 weeks. Neck veins are flat. The most likely diagnosis is:
gi-patho-3:budd-chiari.e: Polycythemia vera is a classic cause of Budd-Chiari syndrome; absent JVD separates it from cardiac causes.

gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.q: A serum-to-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL indicates ascites due to:
gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.e: SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL reflects raised sinusoidal pressure.

gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.q: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the ascitic fluid neutrophil count exceeds:
gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.e: Treat empirically with a third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin.

gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.q: A 61-year-old woman with hepatitis C cirrhosis and ascites becomes confused. Temperature is 37.9 °C and her abdomen is mildly tender. Paracentesis shows 620 neutrophils/mm³; Gram stain shows gram-negative rods of a single type. The organisms most likely reached the fluid by:
o: Ascending infection from the bile ducts
gi-patho-3:ascites-sbp.e: SBP is monomicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella); polymicrobial fluid suggests a perforated viscus.

gi-patho-3:lft.q: An AST:ALT ratio above 2 with AST under 500 U/L is most typical of:
gi-patho-3:lft.e: The others usually push aminotransferases above 1000 U/L.

gi-patho-3:lft.q: An isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase with a normal GGT suggests a source in:
gi-patho-3:lft.e: GGT rises with hepatobiliary disease but not bone disease.

gi-patho-3:lft.q: A 49-year-old man with septic shock required vasopressors for 6 hours. The next day AST is 4800 U/L and ALT 4200 U/L; bilirubin is 1.4 mg/dL. Three days later the aminotransferases are falling quickly while bilirubin peaks at 4 mg/dL. The most likely diagnosis is:
gi-patho-3:lft.e: Shock liver: abrupt, very high aminotransferases with rapid fall and a delayed bilirubin peak.

gi-patho-3:hep-sero.q: During the window period of acute hepatitis B, the only positive marker is usually:
gi-patho-3:hep-sero.e: HBsAg has disappeared and anti-HBs is not yet detectable.

gi-patho-3:hep-sero.q: Which serologic profile indicates immunity from vaccination?
gi-patho-3:hep-sero.e: Vaccine contains only HBsAg, so no core antibody forms.

gi-patho-3:hep-sero.q: A 31-year-old man born in Vietnam has HBsAg positive, IgG anti-HBc positive, IgM anti-HBc negative, HBeAg positive and anti-HBs negative on two tests 8 months apart. ALT is 96 U/L. This pattern indicates:
o: Chronic infection with active viral replication
Acute infection in the window period
gi-patho-3:hep-sero.e: Persistent HBsAg > 6 months = chronic; HBeAg signals high replication and infectivity.

gi-patho-3:reye.q: The hepatic lesion of Reye syndrome is:
gi-patho-3:reye.e: Mitochondrial injury impairs β-oxidation; inflammation is absent.

gi-patho-3:reye.q: Aspirin is still recommended in children with:
gi-patho-3:reye.e: It is otherwise avoided during viral illnesses.

gi-patho-3:reye.q: A 7-year-old boy recovering from chickenpox was given aspirin for fever. Four days later he has persistent vomiting and becomes lethargic and combative. Glucose is 48 mg/dL, ammonia is high, and AST/ALT are elevated with a normal bilirubin. The underlying defect is:
o: Inhibition of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation
gi-patho-3:reye.e: Reye syndrome: hepatic encephalopathy with cerebral edema.

gi-patho-3:ald.e: It is typical of, but not specific for, alcoholic hepatitis.

gi-patho-3:ald.q: Alcoholic steatosis results largely from a hepatocyte excess of:
gi-patho-3:ald.e: Alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase generate NADH, favoring lipogenesis and blocking fatty acid oxidation.

gi-patho-3:ald.q: A 44-year-old man drinks a bottle of whiskey daily and has had a week of fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. WBC is 16,000/mm³, AST 240 U/L, ALT 90 U/L. A liver biopsy would most likely show:
o: Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular ducts
Ballooned hepatocytes, neutrophils and Mallory hyaline
Portal plasma cell infiltrate with interface hepatitis
gi-patho-3:ald.e: Alcoholic hepatitis; fibrosis is perisinusoidal (chicken wire) starting in zone 3.

gi-patho-3:nafld.q: The condition most closely linked to MASLD (NAFLD) is:
gi-patho-3:nafld.e: It is the hepatic component of the metabolic syndrome.

gi-patho-3:nafld.q: Which finding is required to diagnose steatohepatitis rather than simple steatosis?
o: Fat droplets in at least 5% of hepatocytes
gi-patho-3:nafld.e: NASH/MASH needs steatosis plus ballooning and lobular inflammation; it cannot be told from alcoholic hepatitis histologically.

gi-patho-3:nafld.q: A 52-year-old woman with BMI 36, type 2 diabetes and no alcohol use has ALT 78 U/L and AST 52 U/L. Viral and autoimmune serologies are negative; ultrasound shows a bright liver. Which complication can arise in her even before cirrhosis develops?
gi-patho-3:nafld.e: MASLD raises HCC risk even without cirrhosis.

gi-patho-3:aih.q: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis is associated with antibodies to:
gi-patho-3:aih.e: ANA and ASMA in type 1; anti-LKM-1 in type 2.

gi-patho-3:aih.q: The inflammatory cell that characteristically dominates in autoimmune hepatitis is the:
gi-patho-3:aih.e: Portal and periportal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with interface hepatitis.

gi-patho-3:aih.q: A 28-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has fatigue and ALT 620 U/L. Viral serologies are negative; she takes no drugs. Serum IgG is twice normal and anti–smooth muscle antibody is positive. The most appropriate treatment is:

gi-patho-3:hep-enceph.q: In hepatic encephalopathy, astrocytes swell because they convert ammonia to:
Lactulose lowers blood ammonia mainly by:
o: Trapping it as ammonium in the colon
gi-patho-3:hep-enceph.e: Acidification converts NH₃ to non-absorbable NH₄⁺; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing bacteria.

gi-patho-3:hep-enceph.q: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis is brought in drowsy and disoriented, with a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. His wife says his stools have been black for two days. The most likely precipitant is:
gi-patho-3:hep-enceph.e: Blood in the gut is digested to ammonia.

gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.q: The most common benign tumor of the liver is the:
gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.e: Biopsy is avoided because of bleeding risk.

gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.q: A central stellate scar on imaging is characteristic of:
gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.e: FNH is a non-neoplastic hyperplastic response to a vascular anomaly.

gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.q: A 27-year-old woman who has used oral contraceptives for 9 years has sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. CT shows a 7-cm subcapsular liver mass with hemoperitoneum. The mass is most likely a:
gi-patho-3:liver-tumors.e: Adenomas can rupture; β-catenin–activated ones can become malignant.

gi-patho-3:a1at.q: The hepatocyte inclusions of α1-antitrypsin deficiency are:
gi-patho-3:a1at.e: Misfolded protein retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.

gi-patho-3:a1at.q: Liver disease in α1-antitrypsin deficiency results from:
o: Unopposed elastase activity in the liver
Accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes
gi-patho-3:a1at.e: A toxic gain of function; the lung disease is a loss of function.

gi-patho-3:a1at.q: A 36-year-old woman who has never smoked has progressive dyspnea and basal hyperlucency on chest radiograph. Her brother needed a liver transplant as a child. Her genotype is most likely:
gi-patho-3:a1at.e: Homozygous Z gives about 10% of normal levels: panacinar emphysema and cirrhosis.

gi-patho-3:wilson.q: Wilson disease is caused by mutation of a gene encoding a:
gi-patho-3:wilson.e: ATP7B exports copper into bile and loads it onto ceruloplasmin.

gi-patho-3:wilson.q: The most specific biochemical test for Wilson disease is increased:
gi-patho-3:wilson.e: Ceruloplasmin is low; hepatic copper content is the most sensitive test.

gi-patho-3:wilson.q: A 19-year-old man has a new tremor, slurred speech and personality change. AST and ALT are mildly raised and he has a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Slit-lamp examination would most likely show deposits in:
gi-patho-3:wilson.e: Kayser-Fleischer rings accompany nearly all neurologic Wilson disease.

gi-patho-3:hemochrom.q: Hereditary hemochromatosis increases iron absorption because of low:
gi-patho-3:hemochrom.e: Without hepcidin, ferroportin keeps exporting iron from enterocytes.

gi-patho-3:hemochrom.q: In early hemochromatosis, hemosiderin is first seen in:
gi-patho-3:hemochrom.e: Iron is directly toxic; inflammation is characteristically absent.

gi-patho-3:hemochrom.q: A 52-year-old man has fatigue, loss of libido, new diabetes and painful second and third MCP joints. His skin looks tanned although he avoids the sun. Transferrin saturation is 82%. The best treatment is:
gi-patho-3:hemochrom.e: HFE hemochromatosis; HCC risk stays high even after treatment.

gi-patho-3:jaundice.q: Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that appears during fasting or illness in an otherwise well adult suggests:
Which disorder causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a grossly black liver?
gi-patho-3:jaundice.e: Defective canalicular excretion; Rotor is similar but without the pigment.

gi-patho-3:jaundice.q: A 5-week-old girl has had jaundice since the second week of life, with dark urine and pale stools. Direct bilirubin is 6.8 mg/dL and GGT is high. Ultrasound cannot identify a gallbladder. The most likely diagnosis is:
gi-patho-3:jaundice.e: Fibro-obliteration of extrahepatic ducts; commonest indication for pediatric liver transplantation.

gi-patho-3:psc-pbc.q: Antimitochondrial antibodies in primary biliary cholangitis target:
The cholangiographic hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis is:
o: Beading from alternating strictures and dilations
Filling defects in a normal-caliber duct
gi-patho-3:psc-pbc.e: Concentric periductal 'onion-skin' fibrosis is the histologic counterpart.

gi-patho-3:psc-pbc.q: A 47-year-old woman has had itching for a year and fatigue. She has xanthelasmas. ALP is 480 U/L, bilirubin normal. Ultrasound shows normal bile ducts. Liver biopsy would most likely show:
o: Lymphocytic and granulomatous destruction of small bile ducts
Concentric fibrosis around large bile ducts
Bile plugs in dilated canaliculi with neutrophils
gi-patho-3:psc-pbc.e: PBC: florid duct lesions; treat with ursodeoxycholic acid.

gi-patho-3:gallstones.q: Black pigment gallstones are most associated with:
gi-patho-3:gallstones.e: Excess unconjugated bilirubin forms calcium bilirubinate.

gi-patho-3:gallstones.q: Non-visualization of the gallbladder on HIDA scan indicates:
gi-patho-3:gallstones.e: The tracer cannot enter the gallbladder in acute cholecystitis.

gi-patho-3:gallstones.q: A 72-year-old woman has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. She is confused and her blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct. After fluids and antibiotics, the most important next step is:
o: HIDA scan to confirm the diagnosis
gi-patho-3:gallstones.e: Reynolds pentad: suppurative ascending cholangitis needs decompression.

gi-patho-3:biliary-ca.q: A risk factor shared by cholangiocarcinoma worldwide is infection with:
gi-patho-3:biliary-ca.e: Clonorchis and Opisthorchis; PSC is the other major risk.

gi-patho-3:biliary-ca.q: The most important risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma is:
gi-patho-3:biliary-ca.e: Stones are present in 95% of cases, though only 1–2% of people with stones develop cancer.

gi-patho-3:biliary-ca.q: A 38-year-old man with long-standing ulcerative colitis and an elevated alkaline phosphatase for years has new painless jaundice and weight loss. MRCP shows a dominant stricture at the confluence of the hepatic ducts. CA 19-9 is high. The most likely diagnosis is:

gi-patho-3:acute-panc.q: The most specific serum marker of acute pancreatitis is:
gi-patho-3:acute-panc.e: Lipase stays elevated for 8–14 days; amylase normalizes in 3–5 days.

gi-patho-3:acute-panc.q: Hypocalcemia in severe acute pancreatitis results from:
gi-patho-3:acute-panc.e: Fatty acids released by lipase bind calcium.

gi-patho-3:acute-panc.q: A 45-year-old woman has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back after a fatty meal. Lipase is 2400 U/L, ALT 310 U/L, triglycerides 180 mg/dL. She does not drink alcohol. Four weeks later CT shows a 7-cm fluid collection next to the pancreas. Its wall is composed of:
o: Granulation and fibrous tissue without epithelium
gi-patho-3:acute-panc.e: Gallstone pancreatitis complicated by a pseudocyst.

gi-patho-3:chronic-panc.q: The most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults is:
gi-patho-3:chronic-panc.e: Up to 25% of cases have a genetic basis (CFTR, PRSS1, SPINK1).

gi-patho-3:chronic-panc.q: Which finding on abdominal imaging best supports chronic pancreatitis?
A 50-year-old man with 20 years of heavy drinking has recurrent epigastric pain, 10-kg weight loss and bulky, oily stools. Amylase and lipase are normal. Which test result is most expected?
gi-patho-3:chronic-panc.e: Exocrine insufficiency appears when under 10% of function remains; enzymes may be normal because acini are lost.

gi-patho-3:panc-ca.q: The most frequently mutated gene in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is:
gi-patho-3:panc-ca.e: An early event in PanIN; CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 follow.

gi-patho-3:panc-ca.q: The strongest environmental risk factor for pancreatic cancer is:
gi-patho-3:panc-ca.e: Chronic pancreatitis and diabetes are also risk factors.

gi-patho-3:panc-ca.q: A 66-year-old man has 6 weeks of painless jaundice, pruritus, pale stools and 7-kg weight loss. A smooth, non-tender mass is felt under the right costal margin. He recently had tender red cords on his left arm and then his right leg. The most likely diagnosis is:

gi-physio:regs.q: Which GI hormone is released by S cells in response to a duodenal pH below about 4.5?
gi-physio:regs.e: Acid in the duodenum releases secretin, which drives pancreatic and biliary HCO₃⁻ secretion.

gi-physio:regs.q: The cyclic release of motilin during fasting is responsible for:
o: Receptive relaxation of the gastric fundus
Phase III of the migrating motor complex
Contraction of the gallbladder after meals
gi-physio:regs.e: Motilin rises just before phase III of the MMC; it has no role in the fed pattern.

gi-physio:regs.q: Fatty acids and amino acids entering the duodenum stimulate I cells. The resulting hormone does all of the following EXCEPT:
gi-physio:regs.e: CCK contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, stimulates enzyme secretion and inhibits gastric emptying.

gi-physio:regs.q: A 48-year-old woman has 3 L/day of watery diarrhea, K⁺ 2.6 mEq/L and very low gastric acid output. CT shows a pancreatic tail mass. The tumor most likely secretes:
gi-physio:regs.e: VIPoma causes Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia and Achlorhydria (WDHA).

gi-physio:secprod.q: Intrinsic factor is secreted by which gastric cell?
gi-physio:secprod.e: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor.

gi-physio:secprod.q: Pepsinogen is converted to active pepsin by:
gi-physio:secprod.e: H⁺ cleaves pepsinogen to pepsin; pepsin is inactive above pH ~5.

gi-physio:secprod.q: Gastrin increases acid secretion mainly by acting on:
gi-physio:secprod.e: Gastrin's main effect is via ECL histamine rather than a direct parietal cell action.

gi-physio:secprod.q: A 62-year-old woman with vitiligo has achlorhydria and a megaloblastic anemia. Gastric biopsy shows loss of oxyntic glands in the body with sparing of the antrum. Secretion of which product is also lost?
gi-physio:secprod.e: Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells → no acid and no IF (pernicious anemia); antral G cells are spared.

gi-physio:parietal.q: Histamine stimulates the parietal cell through which pathway?
gi-physio:parietal.e: H2 couples to Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.

gi-physio:parietal.q: Somatostatin reduces acid secretion by binding a receptor coupled to:
gi-physio:parietal.e: Somatostatin and prostaglandins act through Gi on the parietal cell.

gi-physio:parietal.q: The 'alkaline tide' after a meal results from:
o: Pancreatic HCO₃⁻ absorbed in the jejunum
Brunner gland HCO₃⁻ entering the blood
Basolateral HCO₃⁻ exit from parietal cells
gi-physio:parietal.e: For each H⁺ secreted, HCO₃⁻ leaves basolaterally via Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange, raising gastric venous pH.

gi-physio:parietal.q: A 45-year-old man has taken a proton pump inhibitor daily for 5 years. Which change in fasting plasma values is expected?
gi-physio:parietal.e: Low acid removes D-cell somatostatin inhibition of G cells → hypergastrinemia.

gi-physio:parietal.q: A 38-year-old man has multiple jejunal ulcers and diarrhea despite high-dose PPI. Fasting gastrin is high and rises further after IV secretin. Why does acid stay high despite very low gastric pH?
o: Vagal tone is abolished by the high gastrin
Parietal cells lack H2 receptors in this disorder
Tumor gastrin is not suppressed by somatostatin
gi-physio:parietal.e: Gastrinoma secretion escapes pH/somatostatin feedback; normal G cells would be shut off.

gi-physio:panc.q: As pancreatic secretory rate rises under secretin, the juice shows:
gi-physio:panc.e: Cl⁻ is exchanged for HCO₃⁻ in the ducts; Na⁺ and K⁺ stay near constant.

gi-physio:panc.q: Secretin stimulates ductal HCO₃⁻ secretion mainly by opening which apical channel?
gi-physio:panc.e: cAMP/PKA opens CFTR; Cl⁻ recycles through SLC26 Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange.

gi-physio:panc.q: Trypsinogen is first activated in the duodenum by:
gi-physio:panc.e: Enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen; trypsin then activates other zymogens.

gi-physio:panc.q: A 9-year-old with cystic fibrosis has steatorrhea. Duodenal aspirate after secretin shows a small volume with low HCO₃⁻. The primary defect in his pancreatic ducts is reduced:
o: Apical Cl⁻ available for HCO₃⁻ exchange
gi-physio:panc.e: Without CFTR, luminal Cl⁻ is lacking for Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange, so HCO₃⁻ and water fall and protein plugs form.

gi-physio:carb.q: Fructose enters the enterocyte across the apical membrane via:
gi-physio:carb.e: Fructose uses GLUT5; all three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2.

gi-physio:carb.q: The end products of α-amylase action on starch include all of the following EXCEPT:
gi-physio:carb.e: α-Amylase does not cleave terminal α-1,4 or α-1,6 links, so free glucose is not produced.

gi-physio:carb.q: A 30-year-old man has bloating and diarrhea after milk. Stool pH is low and breath hydrogen rises 40 ppm after lactose. Small-bowel biopsy would most likely show:
gi-physio:carb.e: Primary lactase non-persistence leaves villi normal; the lactose is fermented in the colon.

gi-physio:carb.q: A patient with chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea has a normal urinary D-xylose test. This result best supports:
gi-physio:carb.e: D-xylose needs no digestion; normal uptake means intact proximal mucosa, pointing to maldigestion.

gi-physio:prot.q: Di- and tripeptides are taken up by enterocytes mainly through:
gi-physio:prot.e: PepT1 is an H⁺/oligopeptide cotransporter; cytosolic peptidases finish digestion.

gi-physio:prot.q: Pepsin is important for meat digestion because it uniquely digests:
gi-physio:prot.e: Pepsin digests collagen in connective tissue, letting other enzymes penetrate meat.

gi-physio:prot.q: An infant has failure to thrive, diarrhea and hypoproteinemia. Duodenal fluid contains normal trypsinogen but no trypsin activity, which appears when enteropeptidase is added. The deficient enzyme normally resides in the:
gi-physio:prot.e: Congenital enterokinase deficiency: zymogens are present but never activated.

gi-physio:fat.q: Chylomicrons leave the enterocyte and enter the:
gi-physio:fat.e: Long-chain fats travel in lymph; short/medium-chain fatty acids go directly to portal blood.

gi-physio:fat.q: Without bile salt micelles, the fraction of dietary fat absorbed falls to roughly:
gi-physio:fat.e: Micelles ferry MAG and FFA across the unstirred layer; absorption ~97% with them, 40–50% without.

gi-physio:fat.q: Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides mainly to:
o: Glycerol and three free fatty acids
gi-physio:fat.e: Lipase with colipase cleaves positions 1 and 3.

gi-physio:fat.q: A 4-year-old has steatorrhea, ataxia, night blindness and acanthocytes. Plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are very low and jejunal enterocytes are filled with lipid droplets. The defect is in:
o: Bile acid synthesis in the liver
gi-physio:fat.e: Abetalipoproteinemia (MTP defect): fat cannot be packaged into chylomicrons.

gi-physio:absorb.q: Nonheme iron is reduced and taken up at the duodenal apical membrane by:
gi-physio:absorb.e: Dcytb reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺; DMT1 cotransports Fe²⁺ with H⁺.

gi-physio:absorb.q: Hepcidin lowers intestinal iron absorption by:
o: Blocking DMT1 at the apical border
Binding iron in the intestinal lumen
gi-physio:absorb.e: Hepcidin internalizes and degrades ferroportin; IL-6 raises hepcidin in inflammation.

gi-physio:absorb.q: Folate is absorbed mainly in the:
gi-physio:absorb.e: Brush-border conjugase and folate uptake occur in the proximal small intestine.

gi-physio:absorb.q: Two years after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, a 41-year-old woman has a microcytic anemia with low ferritin. The main reason is that food now bypasses the:
gi-physio:absorb.e: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum ("Iron fist, Bro"); bypass also reduces acid.

gi-physio:b12.q: In the stomach, freed vitamin B12 first binds to:
gi-physio:b12.e: Acid favors binding to haptocorrin; IF binds B12 only after pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin in the duodenum.

gi-physio:b12.q: The IF–B12 complex is absorbed in the:
gi-physio:b12.e: Ileal receptors (Ca²⁺-dependent) take up IF–B12; B12 exits bound to transcobalamin II.

gi-physio:b12.q: A 70-year-old woman has megaloblastic anemia and decreased vibration sense. Which result best separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?
gi-physio:b12.e: MMA rises only with B12 deficiency; homocysteine rises in both.

gi-physio:b12.q: A man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and borderline-low B12. The B12 is low because without pancreatic enzymes:
o: Parietal cells stop secreting intrinsic factor
B12 cannot be released from food protein
Haptocorrin is not degraded to free B12 for IF
gi-physio:b12.e: Pancreatic proteases are needed to cleave haptocorrin so B12 can bind IF.

gi-physio:peyer.q: Microfold (M) cells over Peyer patches function to:
o: Absorb bile salts in the terminal ileum
Secrete dimeric IgA into the intestinal lumen
Produce mucus over the lymphoid follicle dome
Deliver luminal antigens to immune cells below
gi-physio:peyer.e: M cells sample antigens and deliver them to dendritic cells and lymphocytes.

gi-physio:peyer.q: Secretory IgA crosses the intestinal epithelium by:
o: Binding to FcRn in the apical membrane
Exocytosis directly from lamina propria plasma cells
Transcytosis bound to the polymeric Ig receptor
gi-physio:peyer.e: Dimeric IgA binds pIgR basolaterally; cleaved pIgR remains as secretory component.

gi-physio:peyer.q: Peyer patches are found mainly in the:
gi-physio:peyer.e: Unencapsulated lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria/submucosa of the ileum.

gi-physio:peyer.q: A 28-year-old has recurrent sinusitis and giardiasis. Serum IgA is undetectable, IgG and IgM are normal. Which normal mucosal process is impaired?
o: Class switching to IgG in germinal centers
Antibody transcytosis into the gut lumen
gi-physio:peyer.e: Without IgA there is nothing for pIgR to carry into secretions, so mucosal defense suffers.

gi-physio:bile.q: The rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis is:
Conjugated bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by:
gi-physio:bile.e: Apical Na⁺-dependent bile acid transporter; NTCP takes them up into hepatocytes.

gi-physio:bile.q: The strongest stimulus for gallbladder contraction is:
o: Secretin released by acid in the duodenum
CCK released by fat in the duodenum
gi-physio:bile.e: CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

gi-physio:bile.q: After resection of 150 cm of terminal ileum for Crohn disease, a man develops steatorrhea and calcium oxalate kidney stones. The stones form because:
o: Bile salts deplete urinary citrate excretion
Short bowel increases hepatic oxalate synthesis
Unabsorbed fat binds Ca²⁺, freeing oxalate to be absorbed
Vitamin D deficiency increases urinary Ca²⁺
gi-physio:bile.e: Ca²⁺ saponifies with fat, leaving oxalate soluble and absorbable in the colon.

gi-physio:bili.q: Bilirubin is converted to its water-soluble form in hepatocytes by:
gi-physio:bili.e: UGT1A1 forms mono- and diglucuronides (direct bilirubin).

gi-physio:bili.q: Urobilinogen is formed from conjugated bilirubin by:
gi-physio:bili.e: Gut bacteria deconjugate and reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen; some is reabsorbed and excreted as urobilin.

gi-physio:bili.q: Bilirubin in the urine indicates elevated serum:
gi-physio:bili.e: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered.

gi-physio:bili.q: A 22-year-old man becomes mildly jaundiced during a 3-day fast. Indirect bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL; CBC, reticulocytes and liver enzymes are normal. The underlying defect is:
gi-physio:bili.e: Gilbert syndrome: promoter variant with UGT1A1 at 10–33% of normal; benign.

gi-physio:bili.q: A woman has painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and a palpable gallbladder. Which urine finding is expected?
gi-physio:bili.e: Complete obstruction stops bilirubin reaching the gut, so no urobilinogen forms.

gi-physio:motil.q: The basic electrical rhythm of the stomach is about:
gi-physio:motil.e: Slow waves: ~3/min stomach, ~12 duodenum, 8–9 ileum, set by interstitial cells of Cajal.

gi-physio:motil.q: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter during swallowing is mediated mainly by:
gi-physio:motil.e: Inhibitory myenteric neurons release VIP and NO.

gi-physio:motil.q: Which duodenal content most strongly slows gastric emptying through CCK?
gi-physio:motil.e: Fat releases CCK, the most potent hormonal brake on emptying.

gi-physio:motil.q: A 40-year-old has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Manometry shows absent distal peristalsis and incomplete LES relaxation. The underlying lesion is loss of:
o: Cholinergic fibers of the vagus nerve
Interstitial cells of Cajal in the antrum
Inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
Striated muscle of the upper esophagus
gi-physio:motil.e: Achalasia: degeneration of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons in Auerbach's plexus.

o: The longitudinal and circular muscle layers
The submucosa and circular muscle layer
The serosa and longitudinal muscle layer
The mucosa and the submucosal layer
gi-physio:ens.e: Myenteric plexus mainly controls motility; the submucosal plexus controls secretion and blood flow.

gi-physio:ens.q: Sympathetic stimulation reduces gut motility mainly by:
gi-physio:ens.e: NE acts largely on enteric neurons; it also directly relaxes muscle slightly.

gi-physio:ens.q: A newborn fails to pass meconium for 48 hours. Rectal biopsy shows absent ganglion cells. The aganglionic segment is narrowed because it:
o: Is compressed by a hypertrophied sphincter
Has excess interstitial cells of Cajal
Lacks smooth muscle in its wall
Cannot relax, lacking inhibitory enteric neurons
gi-physio:ens.e: Hirschsprung disease: failed neural crest migration (e.g., RET); proximal colon dilates.

steps.q: Gastrin raises acid output mainly by acting on:
steps.e: Gastrin acts on CCK₂ receptors of ECL cells; histamine then stimulates parietal H₂ receptors. It also has a smaller direct effect on parietal cells.

steps.e: Secretin normally inhibits gastrin release from G cells, but gastrinoma cells respond with a paradoxical rise.

steps.q: Steatorrhea here is best explained by:
o: Loss of bile acids in the ileum
steps.e: Excess acid overwhelms pancreatic HCO₃⁻; lipase is irreversibly inactivated at low pH and bile acids precipitate.

Splenic vein to the left renal vein
Superior rectal to the middle rectal veins

Increased nitrogen load from blood in the gut
steps.e: GI bleeding delivers protein to gut bacteria, raising ammonia; lactulose and rifaximin lower it.
